subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does the term 'media' refer to in art and design?
options: The materials and tools used to create an artwork
The final grade awarded for a piece
The gallery where work is displayed
The written evaluation of a project
questions.explain: Media are the physical materials and tools, such as charcoal, paint or clay, that an artist uses to make work.

questions.q: Which of these is a dry drawing medium?
options: Charcoal
Watercolour
Acrylic
Ink wash
questions.explain: Charcoal is a dry medium, whereas watercolour, acrylic and ink wash are all wet media.

options: Assembling and gluing different materials such as paper onto a surface
Carving into a block of lino
Blending colours smoothly with a brush
Firing clay in a kiln
questions.explain: Collage builds an image by sticking down materials like cut paper, fabric or photographs onto a support.

questions.q: Why might a student experiment with a range of media in an exploratory portfolio?
options: To find the most effective materials and techniques for expressing their ideas
To avoid having to record any observations
To ensure every page uses the same material
To reduce the amount of practical work required
questions.explain: Exploring varied media lets students discover which materials best communicate their intentions and refine their work.

questions.q: A student wants a soft, luminous effect with colours that blend into one another on wet paper. Which medium best suits this?
options: Watercolour
Oil pastel on card
Biro pen
Lino print
questions.explain: Watercolour applied to wet paper allows transparent colours to bleed and blend, creating soft luminous effects.

questions.q: A student wants to create multiple identical prints of a bold, high-contrast design. Which technique is most appropriate?
options: Lino printing
Fine pencil shading
Watercolour washes
Smudged charcoal drawing
questions.explain: Lino printing is a relief process ideal for producing repeated, bold, high-contrast images from one carved block.

questions.q: A student's page looks flat and lacks a sense of form. Which technique would most directly improve this?
options: Adding tonal shading to show light and shadow
Writing a longer artist biography
Using only outlines with no shading
Reducing the number of media used
questions.explain: Tone created through shading suggests light and shadow, giving objects a three-dimensional sense of form.

questions.q: In art and design, what is a 'primary source'?
options: Something observed and recorded first-hand by the student
An image copied from the internet
A printed reproduction in a textbook
A description written by another artist
questions.explain: A primary source is material the student gathers directly, such as their own photographs or observational drawings.

questions.q: What is a 'preparatory study' or 'development' in a portfolio?
options: Work that explores and refines ideas before a final outcome
The mounted final piece only
A written examination paper
The list of assessment objectives
questions.explain: Preparatory studies show the process of experimenting with and developing ideas leading towards a final response.

questions.q: Which element records ideas and observations directly from what is in front of you?
options: Observational drawing
Copying a finished poster
A group discussion only
A blank sketchbook page
questions.explain: Observational drawing records ideas, observations and insights first-hand from direct study of a subject.

questions.q: Why is it important to record ideas as work progresses rather than only at the end?
options: It shows the development of thinking and how decisions were made
It guarantees a higher mark automatically
It removes the need for a final piece
It means fewer media need to be tried
questions.explain: Recording throughout demonstrates the journey of ideas and the reasoning behind creative decisions.

questions.q: What does 'refining' ideas in a portfolio mean?
options: Improving and developing work by making considered changes
Copying the same image repeatedly without change
Discarding all earlier sketches
Writing only about other artists
questions.explain: Refining involves selecting and reworking ideas thoughtfully to strengthen the outcome.

questions.q: How does a mood board or theme page help develop ideas?
options: It gathers visual references and inspiration to focus a direction
It replaces the need for any practical work
It provides the final assessment grade
It records only the artist's date of birth
questions.explain: A mood board collects images, colours and references that inspire and shape the direction of a project.

questions.q: A student has one strong drawing but no evidence of how the idea grew. What should they add?
options: A series of developmental sketches and experiments showing the idea evolving
A single unrelated photograph
A copy of the mark scheme
A blank page for balance
questions.explain: Developmental sketches evidence how an idea was explored and refined over time towards the outcome.

questions.q: When responding to an artist, what should a student do beyond simply copying their work?
options: Analyse the artist's techniques and use them to inform their own ideas
Trace the artwork and present it as their own final piece
Only write the artist's full name
Avoid mentioning the artist entirely
questions.explain: A meaningful response studies an artist's methods and applies that understanding to develop personal work.

questions.q: What is meant by 'critical understanding' of sources?
options: Analysing and forming informed opinions about the work you study
Memorising titles without thinking about them
Ignoring the context of an artwork
Only listing the materials used
questions.explain: Critical understanding means examining sources thoughtfully and drawing informed conclusions about them.

questions.q: Why should a student analyse an artist's use of colour and composition?
options: To understand techniques they can apply to their own work
To copy the exact painting for their final piece
To fill space with unrelated writing
To avoid making any practical work
questions.explain: Analysing colour and composition builds knowledge of visual language that can inform a student's own responses.

questions.q: What makes a response to a source 'personal and meaningful'?
options: It reflects the student's own ideas and intentions, not just imitation
It reproduces the source exactly with no changes
It uses only the artist's original title
It contains no development work
questions.explain: A personal response develops the student's own interpretation and intentions rather than merely copying a source.

questions.q: A student admires Van Gogh's expressive brushwork. How should they best respond in their portfolio?
options: Experiment with their own expressive marks inspired by his techniques
Print and glue in a poster of Sunflowers as the outcome
Write only his dates and nationality
Copy the painting exactly using tracing
questions.explain: Applying an artist's approach to one's own experiments shows genuine engagement rather than direct copying.

specSource: CCEA GCSE Art and Design (2017) specification; Component 1: Exploratory Portfolio
